terms.gloss: on this assumption, this being taken as given
evidence: Cic. Div. 1.118: hōc autem positō atque concessō
terms.comment: Latin usually makes an assumption a verb: what one lays down (pōnere) or takes (sūmere) as given, with an accusative and infinitive (see assume). Positum sit, let it be taken as given (Cic. Or. 14, Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: an assumption, a premise (in an argument)
terms.comment: Cicero’s Latin for the logicians’ λήμματα; a word of argument, not of conversation (see premise).

terms.gloss: a belief held without proof, a supposition
evidence: Cic. Fragm. Scaur. 7: apud hominēs barbarōs opīniō plūs valet saepe quam rēs ipsa (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: An assumption in the sense of a belief that may be wrong (see opinion).

phrases.latin: dēmus tibi istās duās sūmptiōnēs, ea quae λήμματα appellant dialecticī; sed nōs Latīnē loquī mālumus
phrases.english: let us grant you those two assumptions, which the logicians call lemmata; but we prefer to speak Latin
but once this is assumed and granted

sources: Lewis & Short: pono · Lewis & Short: sumptio · Lewis & Short: opinio
